_comment: Intelligence themes — the standing beats Andrew covers. Managed via /admin/intelligence/themes. Each theme's slug is its stable ID and intentionally matches the slugs that cases reference in their topics[] field. sources.whitelist here is THEME-SPECIFIC trusted sources layered ON TOP of the global trusted+blocked lists in Defaults (intelligence-settings.json). Seeded from the daily-briefing skill's per-tab configs and voice grades — fully editable. Read at pipeline startup by briefing-generator/scripts/generate.py — edits here take effect on the next daily run.

keywords: Court of International Trade IEEPA ruling
DOJ notice of appeal CIT tariff
Learning Resources Trump Supreme Court tariff
importer tariff refund receivable SEC filing
themes.guidance_prompt: Cover the full IEEPA tariff-refund landscape and anything that could accelerate, delay, or eliminate refunds: the CBP CAPE refund pipeline, the Section 122 surcharge (hard expiration July 24, 2026), duty-drawback mechanics, and appellate posture on BOTH sides of CIT rulings. Watch government/DOJ appeal signals especially — they use different language than importer challenges (search 'emergency stay Federal Circuit tariff', officials saying they 'strongly disagree' or 'will challenge' a ruling, which often precedes a filing by days). Tariff-rate changes, bilateral deals, and product-exclusion grants can reset the refund math and matter as much as court rulings. Key dockets: V.O.S. Selections v. Trump (Fed. Cir. en banc), Learning Resources v. Trump (S. Ct.), Burlap and Barrel and State of Oregon (Section 122), Atmus Filtration and Euro-Notions (IEEPA refund orders). Statutory anchors: 19 U.S.C. § 2132 (§122), § 1514 (protests), § 1581(i) (CIT jurisdiction), § 1520(d), § 1313 (drawback). Voice: trade-law-grade — a Holland & Knight / Torres Trade Law client alert for GCs, compliance officers, and CFOs who want to know when their money comes back and whether the refund is still happening. Lead with the most consequential development; weave statutory cites into prose.

Flagship matter: Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, 3:24-cv-05417 (N.D. Cal., Judge Martínez-Olguín) — the $1.5B settlement, the largest copyright settlement in U.S. history. Track the parallel AI-copyright docket as a SYSTEM, not isolated cases: Kadrey v. Meta, In re OpenAI Copyright MDL (No. 3143), Authors Guild v. OpenAI, NYT v. OpenAI/Microsoft, Concord/UMG v. Anthropic, Getty v. Stability AI, Thomson Reuters v. Ross, Disney/Universal v. Midjourney, Elsevier v. Meta — cross-references matter most when fair-use frameworks transfer or diverge. Watch settlement administration (claims processing, distribution timeline, publisher-vs-author allocation, fee award, any 9th Cir. objector appeal), new filings, discovery / training-data disclosure orders, and AI licensing deals (comparator pricing is § 107(4) market-harm evidence). International: UK Getty v. Stability appeal, EU AI Act / DSM Directive Art. 4 TDM exception. Statutory anchors: 17 U.S.C. § 107 (fair-use four factors), § 504 (statutory damages), § 411 (registration prerequisite). Voice: litigation-grade — a Davis Polk / Paul Weiss client alert, not a marketing post. Audience: creditor-side claims investors and rights-holder counsel, not retail authors.

Covers the post-2022 crypto-insolvency wave and emerging 2025-26 cases, focused on creditor-rights and customer-property issues. Key open dockets: BlockFills (Ch. 11, customer-rights echoing Celsius), Synapse/Mercury/Evolve embedded-fintech failures, the FTX claim-trading aftermarket, Prime Trust receivership, Genesis/DCG appellate posture, and Three Arrows Capital (Hong Kong / BVI / Singapore liquidator coordination). The central question across cases: are customer crypto deposits property of the estate or held in trust/bailment (Celsius's contested TOS litigation; Gatecoin, HKCFI 914). Also track claim-valuation-date disputes (in-kind vs. fiat, petition-date vs. distribution-date), token/asset tracing, fraudulent-transfer claims against insiders (FTX/Alameda model), and plan/distribution mechanics. Statutory anchors: 11 U.S.C. § 541 (property of estate), § 363 (sales), § 1129 (confirmation); offshore: HK CWUMPO, Cayman Companies Act Part V, BVI Insolvency Act 2003. Voice: restructuring-grade — a Paul Hastings / Akin Gump alert. Pattern recognition across dockets matters more than depth on any single case.

Tracks active receiverships, clawback litigation, and cross-border asset recovery from the claims-buying perspective — recovery trajectory, distribution timing, and clawback risk for net winners. Key ongoing dockets: Madoff / Picard SIPC trustee (16+ years distributing; fee disputes continue), Stanford receiver (US/UK/Antigua coordination), BitConnect international tracing, OneCoin / Ruja Ignatova, and SEC-enforcement-driven receiverships. Recurring themes: clawback exposure under 11 U.S.C. § 548 and state UFTA/UVTA (net winners face real risk; Ponzi-presumption rulings); multi-jurisdictional distribution timing (cases routinely take 5-15 years; claim trading prices the time value); and fee creep (major receiver/counsel fee orders are signal events for claim pricing). Watch new SEC/DOJ enforcement + receiver appointments, whistleblower awards (an early signal of the next wave, often months before charges), cross-border tracing tools (Mareva injunctions, Norwich Pharmacal / Bankers Trust orders, 28 U.S.C. § 1782, MLAT requests), and crypto/digital-asset tracing with victim-restitution components. Anchors: § 548, state UFTA/UVTA, SEC Act § 21, FRCP 66; UK § 423 Insolvency Act 1986, CPR 25 (Mareva). Voice: recovery-grade — between a Kobre & Kim asset-recovery alert and a Quinn Emanuel distressed memo; audience is sophisticated claims investors and fund LPs.

keywords: Google advertiser mass arbitration Keller Postman
themes.guidance_prompt: Tracks mega-settlements (>$1B) across all class-action verticals PLUS Big Tech mass arbitration. Settlement lenses: notice & claims rate (lower filing rates = higher per-claim recovery for filers), objector campaigns and appellate exposure, fee-award trajectory (percentage-of-fund vs. lodestar cross-check), distribution timing, and opt-out vs. claims-made structure (the denominator math for valuing tradeable claims). Verticals: securities (10b-5, §11, SPAC), ERISA excessive-fee, antitrust price-fixing MDLs, mass torts (opioids, talc / J&J Texas Two-Step, PFAS 3M/DuPont, Roundup, Camp Lejeune), privacy (BIPA, TCPA, data breach), and wildfire/environmental (PG&E). Catch pre-settlement signals (mediator appointments, stayed trial dates, joint status reports) — they precede announcements by weeks. Mass arbitration: flagship Google advertiser arbitration (Keller Postman / Warren Postman; ~$218B exposure) built on DOJ v. Google predicate findings (E.D. Va. adtech, Judge Brinkema; D.D.C. search, Judge Mehta) plus the publisher track (USA Today, Daily Mail, Advance, Magnite, PubMatic); watch the AAA Mass Arbitration Supplementary Rules, bellwether/batching rulings, and the pivot from fighting every claim to global settlement. Anchors: FRCP 23, CAFA, PSLRA; Sherman Act §§ 1-2, Clayton Act § 4 (treble), FAA (Concepcion, Epic Systems, Coinbase v. Bielski). Monitor Cornerstone/NERA reports and the Stanford Securities Class Action Clearinghouse. Voice: litigation-grade; audience: institutional claim filers, fund LPs, opt-out plaintiff counsel. (AI-copyright mega-settlements like Bartz are primary-covered under LLM/Copyright; cross-reference here when >$1B.)

Tracks appellate-level bankruptcy doctrine that changes creditor recoveries — not run-of-the-mill Ch. 11 filings. Key doctrinal areas: third-party / non-debtor releases post-Harrington v. Purdue Pharma (603 U.S. ___ (2024)) — how lower courts apply the consent and statutory-authority limits; equitable mootness (circuit splits on review of confirmed plans; any SCOTUS interest); structured dismissals and gifting (Czyzewski v. Jevic progeny); Texas Two-Step / divisional mergers (In re LTL Management and Bestwall aftermath; good-faith dismissals); mass-tort channeling injunctions (§ 524(g) asbestos vs. expanding § 105(a)); § 363 free-and-clear (successor liability / tort-claim discharge boundaries); and DIP/priming fights plus avoidance actions (§ 547 preference, § 548 fraudulent transfer). Frame every doctrinal shift in terms of recovery economics, not pure legal theory. Key fora: S.D.N.Y., D. Del., S.D. Tex., N.D. Ill.; 2nd/3rd/5th Circuits; Supreme Court (rare but high-impact — Purdue, Jevic, Stern v. Marshall). Anchors: 11 U.S.C. § 105(a), § 363, § 502, § 524, § 547, § 1129, § 1141. Voice: restructuring-grade; audience: creditor-side claims investors, distressed funds, lender-side counsel. (Crypto Ch. 11 plan-confirmation doctrine cross-references Crypto Insolvency.)
